all_of: a reverse proxy denies one path prefix and the application behind it trusts every request the proxy forwards
a route returns the status code of a URL the attacker chose
a second route behind the proxy deny rule runs a fetch with no scheme or host filter
any_of: the fetch is execFile curl with the URL as an argument
an internal datastore listens with authentication disabled
an admin-only route interpolates parsed certificate fields into a database query

chain.action: read the proxy config for the denied prefix and the app for the route it protects; confirm the app never re-checks the path
chain.why: the deny rule is the only control, so the whole chain is about reaching that route once

chain.action: test percent-encoded and dot-segment forms of the denied path against both the proxy and the app
chain.why: HAProxy 2.2 does not decode or normalise, and Node truncates at the fragment, so no path string is denied by one and accepted by the other; rule this out before spending time on it

chain.action: point the status-mirroring route at an attacker server that answers a bare 101 Switching Protocols, with no Upgrade and no Connection header, on a non-default port
chain.why: the app mirrors 101 to the proxy, the proxy reads a successful upgrade and stops parsing HTTP on that connection; the headers must be absent or the Node client raises upgrade instead of response and the fetch never resolves

chain.action: write the second request onto the same socket immediately, addressed to the denied path
chain.why: the proxy is in tunnel mode and forwards raw bytes, so the ACL is never evaluated; the backend keep-alive timeout closes the socket within seconds

chain.action: send gopher at a byte logger you control and read what actually arrived before building any wire-protocol payload
chain.why: whether curl transmits NUL bytes in a gopher selector is version-dependent, and the channel is blind so a wrong assumption is invisible

chain.action: send one OP_MSG update over gopher to the unauthenticated datastore to set the account's permission field, then log in again
chain.why: registration hardcodes the low-privilege role and no admin is seeded; the session copies the permission at login, so the old session stays unprivileged

chain.action: submit a certificate whose issuer commonName opens a block comment after overwriting the stored path field, and whose organizationName closes it
chain.why: each field is interpolated on its own line, so a line comment cannot reach the real path field; the block comment swallows it and leaves the rest of the map literal valid

chain.action: shape the injected path as /a";<command>;"/b so that dirname drops the last segment and the archiver's quoted directory argument closes on the injected quote
chain.why: the archive library calls execFile with shell true and interpolates the directory into a quoted argument, so the joined shell string runs the command

chain.action: copy the flag into the directory the app serves statically, using a glob for its randomised name, and fetch it
chain.why: the execution is blind, so the read-back has to go through a channel the app already exposes

first_confirming_probe.request: GET /healthcheck?url=http://<your-host>:<non-default-port>/ where that host answers a bare 101, then on the same socket GET /healthcheck-dev?url=http://127.0.0.1:3000/
first_confirming_probe.expected: the first request returns 101 and the second returns an application response instead of the proxy's 403
first_confirming_probe.falsifier: the first request returns 504 (the 101 carried Upgrade/Connection and the client hung), or the second still returns 403 (the proxy did not enter tunnel mode)

blast_radius: steps 6 to 8 write: one datastore document is modified, one graph node is created and a shell command runs as the application user. Pin the datastore update to your own account by username and never use a match-all filter. The shell command should write to a path you introduced, not overwrite an application file. Remove the written file and the archiver's temporary archives afterwards with a second injected certificate.

verification.evidence: HTTP 200 from GET /static/js/zz.txt whose body was the flag copied out of /flag<random>.txt on the live target

reuse_when: a reverse proxy ACL is the only thing protecting a route and path-shape bypasses have been ruled out
an endpoint reflects the status code of a URL the attacker supplies
a fetch helper passes an attacker-controlled URL to curl with no scheme filter
a library calls execFile or spawn with shell true and interpolates a path into a quoted argument
known_traps: a 101 carrying Upgrade and Connection makes a Node client raise the upgrade event, so the fetch never resolves and the proxy answers 504
a URL whose port parseInt-s to NaN is rejected, and Node's URL normalises a default port to the empty string, so the listener needs an explicit non-default port
the backend keep-alive timeout closes the tunnelled socket, so the second request must follow the 101 with no delay
an application 500 closes the connection, so one tunnel carries one probe
curl transmits NUL bytes in a gopher selector at 7.70.0 but rejects them with CURLE_URL_MALFORMAT at 8.x; measure it on the target, not on the attacking host
gopher makes the status code 000, which becomes status 0 and throws, so a successful request is indistinguishable from a failed one by status alone
a certificate commonName is capped at 64 characters, which constrains the injected path and forces the block-comment form
